subject: Applied Thermodynamics
summary: vapour-compression and air (Bell–Coleman) refrigeration, heat pumps, COP and tonnes of refrigeration, vapour absorption, properties of moist air (specific and relative humidity, enthalpy, wet-bulb and dew point), the psychrometric chart and basic air-conditioning processes with bypass factor
next_day: Engineering Mathematics, Complex Variables & Numerical Methods

questions.text: In a vapour-compression refrigeration cycle, subcooling the liquid refrigerant leaving the condenser (all other states unchanged)
opts: reduces the refrigerating effect
increases the refrigerating effect and the COP without changing the compressor work per kg
increases the compressor work per kg
has no effect on the cycle
questions.ans: (B) increases the refrigerating effect and the COP without changing the compressor work per kg
solution: Concept: The throttle is isenthalpic, so h4 = h3.
Subcooling lowers h<sub>3</sub>, hence h<sub>4</sub>, so the refrigerating effect h<sub>1</sub> − h<sub>4</sub> grows.
Compressor inlet and outlet states are unchanged, so the work per kg is the same: COP rises (B).
Exam tip: A liquid–suction heat exchanger gives subcooling, but the extra suction superheat it causes may raise the work.

questions.text: A reversed Carnot heat pump delivers heat to a room at 50 °C while taking heat from the ground at 5 °C. Its COP (round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: COPHP = TH/(TH − TL), with absolute temperatures.
T<sub>H</sub> = 323.15 K, T<sub>L</sub> = 278.15 K, T<sub>H</sub> − T<sub>L</sub> = 45 K
Exam tip: The refrigerator COP between the same temperatures is 278.15/45 = 6.18, exactly one less.

questions.text: One tonne of refrigeration (1 TR) is defined as the rate of heat removal needed to
opts: cool 1 tonne of water from 100 °C to 0 °C in 24 hours
evaporate 1 tonne of water in 1 hour
freeze 1 short ton (2000 lb) of water at 0 °C into ice at 0 °C in 24 hours
freeze 1 tonne of water in 1 hour
questions.ans: (C) freeze 1 short ton (2000 lb) of water at 0 °C into ice at 0 °C in 24 hours
solution: Concept: The unit comes from the ice industry.
Freezing 907 kg of water at 0 °C (latent heat ≈ 335 kJ/kg) in 24 h needs ≈ 3.5 kW: (C).
1 TR = 211 kJ/min = 3.517 kW (often taken as 3.5 kW).
Exam tip: Always check which value of 1 TR the question gives (3.5 or 3.517 kW).

questions.text: A vapour-compression refrigerator works with these enthalpies: evaporator exit h<sub>1</sub> = 388 kJ/kg, compressor exit h<sub>2</sub> = 421 kJ/kg and condenser exit h<sub>3</sub> = 236 kJ/kg. The COP (round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: COP = refrigerating effect/compressor work = (h1 − h4)/(h2 − h1), with h4 = h3.
Refrigerating effect = 388 − 236 = 152 kJ/kg
Compressor work = 421 − 388 = 33 kJ/kg
Exam tip: The heat rejected in the condenser is h2 − h3 = 185 kJ/kg = 152 + 33, a quick check.

questions.text: The p–h diagram of a simple vapour-compression cycle is shown. The throttling (expansion) process is
solution: Concept: Throttling is isenthalpic, so it is a vertical line (h constant) from high to low pressure on the p–h chart.
3–4 drops from condenser pressure to evaporator pressure at constant h: (A).
1–2 is compression, 2–3 condensation (heat rejection) and 4–1 evaporation (refrigerating effect).
Exam tip: On a T–s chart the throttle is drawn dashed, because it is irreversible.

questions.text: An ideal Bell–Coleman air-refrigeration cycle works with a pressure ratio of 4 (γ = 1.4). Its COP (round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: COP = 1/(rp(γ−1)/γ − 1) for isentropic compression and expansion.
Exam tip: The COP depends only on the pressure ratio; reducing rp raises COP but also cuts the refrigerating effect per kg of air.

questions.text: In an ammonia–water vapour-absorption refrigeration system, the compressor of the vapour-compression system is replaced by
opts: an expansion valve and a condenser
a turbine and an evaporator
a rectifier only
an absorber, a solution pump and a generator
questions.ans: (D) an absorber, a solution pump and a generator
solution: Concept: The absorption system compresses the refrigerant ‘thermally’.
Ammonia vapour is absorbed in weak solution in the absorber, the strong solution is pumped to high pressure, and heat in the generator drives the ammonia off: (D).
Pumping a liquid needs very little work compared with compressing a vapour.
Exam tip: In a LiBr–water system, water is the refrigerant and LiBr the absorbent; in NH3–water, ammonia is the refrigerant.

questions.text: Air at 35 °C and a total pressure of 101.325 kPa has a relative humidity of 40 %. The saturation pressure of water at 35 °C is 5.628 kPa. The specific humidity of the air (in g per kg of dry air, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: pv = φps; ω = 0.622 pv/(p − pv).
Exam tip: Degree of saturation μ = ω/ωs is slightly less than φ (here μ ≈ 0.39).

questions.text: For air–water vapour mixtures at ordinary conditions, the thermodynamic wet-bulb (adiabatic saturation) temperature is practically equal to the wet-bulb temperature read by a psychrometer because
opts: the air is always saturated
the Lewis number for air–water vapour is close to 1
the specific heat of water is constant
the dew point equals the dry-bulb temperature
questions.ans: (B) the Lewis number for air–water vapour is close to 1
solution: Concept: The psychrometric WBT is set by a balance of heat and mass transfer at the wick; the adiabatic saturation temperature by an energy balance.
The two coincide when h/(ρcphm) = Le2/3 ≈ 1, true for air–water: (B).
That is why constant-WBT lines on the chart are (almost) constant-enthalpy lines.
Exam tip: For other gas–liquid pairs (e.g. air–alcohol) the two temperatures differ.

questions.text: Moist air at 30 °C has a specific humidity of 0.015 kg/kg of dry air. Taking h = 1.005t + ω(2500 + 1.88t) kJ/kg of dry air (t in °C), its enthalpy (in kJ/kg of dry air, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Enthalpy of moist air = dry-air sensible part + vapour part (latent at 0 °C + superheat).
Exam tip: More than half of this enthalpy is latent: removing moisture is what loads a cooling coil.

questions.text: The schematic psychrometric chart shows four processes from the state O. Chemical (adsorption) dehumidification, e.g. over silica gel, is best represented by
solution: Concept: In adsorption the vapour gives up its latent heat (plus heat of adsorption) to the air stream.
So ω falls while the dry-bulb temperature rises, roughly along a constant-enthalpy line: down and to the right, O–4 (D).
O–1 is heating with humidification, O–2 humidification at constant DBT and O–3 cooling with dehumidification.
Exam tip: Cooling-coil dehumidification (O–3) cools the air; chemical dehumidification heats it.

questions.text: Air at 30 °C flows over a cooling coil whose apparatus dew point is 12 °C. If the bypass factor of the coil is 0.15, the temperature of the air leaving the coil (in °C, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: BF = (t2 − tADP)/(t1 − tADP): the fraction of air that ‘misses’ the coil surface.
Exam tip: More coil rows or lower air velocity give a smaller bypass factor (higher contact factor 1 − BF).

questions.text: A vapour-absorption refrigerator receives heat in its generator at 100 °C, rejects heat to the surroundings at 30 °C and produces cooling at −10 °C. Its maximum possible COP is about
solution: Concept: Ideal absorption system = reversible heat engine (TG → T0) driving a reversible refrigerator (TE → T0).
Exam tip: Real absorption COPs are about 0.5–0.7: they pay off only with cheap waste heat.

questions.text: Moist air with 1.2 kg/s of dry air and a specific humidity of 0.006 kg/kg is heated from 10 °C to 30 °C in a heating coil. Taking c<sub>p</sub> of dry air = 1.005 and of water vapour = 1.88 kJ/kg·K, the heating load (in kW, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Sensible heating at constant ω uses the humid specific heat cpa + ωcpv.
Humid specific heat = 1.005 + 0.006 × 1.88 = 1.01628 kJ/kg·K
Exam tip: Ignoring the vapour term gives 24.12 kW, which is outside the accepted range here.

questions.text: The refrigerant vapour leaving the evaporator of a practical refrigerator is usually slightly superheated mainly to
opts: raise the condenser pressure
increase the refrigerating effect per kg by a large amount
make sure that no liquid droplets enter the compressor
reduce the compressor discharge temperature
questions.ans: (C) make sure that no liquid droplets enter the compressor
solution: Concept: Liquid entering a reciprocating compressor (slugging) can damage valves and dilute the lubricant.
A few degrees of superheat, controlled by the thermostatic expansion valve, guarantees ‘dry’ compression: (C).
Superheat raises the suction specific volume and the discharge temperature, so it is kept small.
Exam tip: Useful superheat (inside the cold space) adds to the refrigerating effect; superheat in the suction line does not.
